rationale: validation_status=fail with mutation_score=0.833 (>=0.5) and analyzer_status=warning, but the uncovered_requirement issue for SR1 blocks retention per the retain rule (validation must pass). Examining mutant_sr1_condition_negation_001: it genuinely corrupts the reported activation_condition, changing the rare trigger description ('fires only when the counter equals the rare constant AND the round-state matches') into an almost-always-true condition (fires whenever the counter does NOT equal the rare constant, dropping the round-state conjunct entirely). This is a real, observable degradation of the SR1 finding's correctness — a corrupted submission that describes the trigger as near-constant rather than rare should be rejected. Yet validation shows this mutant went undetected (mutants_detected=0 of 1 targeting SR1), meaning the evaluate.py SR1 check is too permissive: it likely only verifies that the signal_name token (e.g. 'trig_cnt') appears with confidence>=0.5, without actually checking that the reported activation_condition semantically matches the rare-match-AND-state-condition (versus an inverted/near-always-true condition). This is a genuine coverage gap in the harness, not a defective mutant.
revision_instructions: Strengthen the SR1 check in evaluate.py so it does not merely look for the trigger signal name at confidence>=0.5, but also validates the semantic direction of the reported activation_condition. Concretely: parse/inspect the finding's activation_condition string and confirm it describes a RARE, conjunctive condition (the free-running counter reaching its specific rare constant AND an existing round/state register equaling a specific value) rather than an inverted or unconditional/near-always-true condition (e.g. 'not equal to', 'always', 'every cycle regardless of state'). A submission whose activation_condition asserts the payload fires whenever the counter differs from the rare constant (i.e., almost every cycle) must FAIL SR1, since it mischaracterizes a rare trigger as a common one. Implement this via a behavioral/content check on the submitted JSON text: check for negation phrases ('not equal', 'except when', 'NOT ==', '!=') applied to the rare-constant comparison, or verify the condition does not drop the required round/state conjunct — do not anchor on exact wording from any specific submission, since correct submissions may phrase the rare condition differently. Add or fix a mutant-detection test case exercising exactly this inverted-condition failure mode and confirm it now fails.
